source.title: The 5 Love Languages
source.attribution: A summary of The 5 Love Languages by Gary Chapman (1992). Not affiliated with or endorsed by the author or publisher.
source.notes: Original summary written by Reborn; contains no text from the book. The book is in copyright.

cards.title: People feel loved in different ways
cards.body:
Chapman's core idea is that people tend to express and recognise love through one main channel. He names five: kind words, focused time together, gifts, helpful actions and physical touch.

Problems arise when two people speak different languages. One partner may work hard to help around the house while the other mostly longs for undivided attention, and both end up feeling unappreciated. Learning which way your partner best receives love lets your effort land where it counts.
cards.apply_it: Ask someone close to you which of the five makes them feel most cared for, and share your own.

quiz.question: Which of these is NOT one of Chapman's five love languages?
options: Words of affirmation
Acts of service
Financial security
Quality time
quiz.explanation: The five are words of affirmation, quality time, receiving gifts, acts of service and physical touch.

cards.title: Keep the emotional 'love tank' topped up
cards.body:
Chapman uses the picture of an emotional tank. When it's full, people feel secure and can handle stress and disagreement more generously. When it's empty, small issues turn into big fights and partners feel distant.

The tank is filled most efficiently by love expressed in the person's main language. That means a regular, small habit of speaking their language often does more than an occasional grand gesture in a language they don't value.
cards.apply_it: Plan one small action in your partner's or friend's love language for each day this week.

quiz.question: What does Chapman's 'love tank' image suggest?
options: People cope better when they regularly feel loved in their own language
Love is limited and runs out for good
Only gifts can fill it
It matters only early in a relationship
quiz.explanation: A full tank makes people more secure; filling it in their language works best.

cards.title: Find someone's love language by noticing their complaints and requests
cards.body:
Chapman suggests a few clues for working out a person's primary language. Look at what they most often ask for, what they complain about when hurt, and how they tend to show love to others.

A frequent complaint like 'we never spend time together' points to quality time, while 'you never notice what I do' may point to words of affirmation. Complaints that feel annoying can actually be useful directions to what the person needs most.
cards.apply_it: Write down the last two complaints or requests someone close to you made. What love language might they point to?

quiz.question: Which clue does Chapman suggest for discovering someone's love language?
options: Their star sign
Their job
How much money they earn
What they complain about and ask for most
quiz.explanation: Repeated complaints and requests often reveal the unmet need.

cards.title: When the early spark fades, love becomes a choice
cards.body:
Chapman describes the excited, obsessive phase of falling in love as real but temporary. When it fades, many couples think something is wrong.

His view is that a deeper kind of love begins here: a deliberate decision to care for the other person, including speaking their language when it doesn't come naturally. Feelings often follow actions, so choosing to love in practical ways can renew warmth that seemed lost.
cards.apply_it: Choose one loving action this week that doesn't come naturally to you, and do it without expecting anything back.

quiz.question: What happens after the 'in love' phase, according to Chapman?
options: The relationship must end
Lasting love relies more on deliberate choices
Gifts must get bigger
Nothing changes
quiz.explanation: He sees mature love as a choice expressed through actions, not just a feeling.

cards.title: Within each language, the details matter
cards.body:
Chapman notes that each love language has 'dialects'. Quality time, for example, isn't just being in the same room; it means undivided attention, such as a real conversation with phones away. Gifts don't need to be expensive; what counts is the thought they show.

So knowing someone's language is only the start. Paying attention to the specific forms that matter to them, like the kind of words, time or help they value, makes your effort truly felt.
cards.apply_it: For someone close to you, write one very specific version of their love language, such as a 20-minute walk with no phones.

quiz.question: According to Chapman, what does real quality time involve?
options: Watching TV together
Being in the same house
Undivided, focused attention
Expensive outings
quiz.explanation: Being nearby isn't enough; focused attention is what makes time together count.

cards.title: Encourage the things your partner is hesitant to try
cards.body:
In describing words of affirmation, Chapman highlights encouragement: words that give someone courage. Many people have an interest or ability they haven't pursued because they're unsure of themselves, such as starting a business, going back to school or writing.

Chapman suggests noticing these hidden hopes and speaking up for them. The aim is to support what the other person wants for themselves, not to push them toward what you want for them. For someone whose language is words, sincere encouragement can mean a great deal.
cards.apply_it: Think of something your partner or friend has mentioned wanting to try. Tell them one specific reason you think they could do it.

quiz.question: What does Chapman mean by encouraging words?
options: Pushing your partner toward goals you've chosen for them
Words that give courage for something they want to pursue
Praising them only in public
Reminding them of past failures so they try harder
quiz.explanation: Encouragement supports the other person's own hopes.

cards.title: Make requests, not demands
cards.body:
Chapman points out that the way we ask for things changes how they land. A demand turns a partner into a servant and invites resistance. A request, said kindly, shows that you value them and recognise that they have a choice.

He argues that love can't be forced. When you tell your partner what you'd appreciate, you give them guidance on how to love you, but they remain free to offer it. That freedom is what makes the response feel like love rather than compliance.
cards.apply_it: Turn one demand you often make, such as 'You need to call me', into a request: 'I'd really love it if you called on your lunch break.'

quiz.question: Why does Chapman prefer requests to demands?
options: Requests are faster
Demands are only fine for big issues
Demands show you care more
Requests guide love while leaving the other person free to give it
quiz.explanation: Love can't be forced; requests leave room for a freely given response.

cards.title: Don't keep bringing up past wrongs
cards.body:
In his discussion of kind words, Chapman addresses forgiveness. He describes how some couples bring past failures into each new argument, so that every disagreement reopens old wounds.

He suggests that real forgiveness is a decision not to hold a confessed wrong against the other person anymore. It doesn't erase the memory or the pain at once, but it stops using the past as a weapon. Without that choice, he argues, a relationship struggles to move forward. Forgiveness is for wrongs that are acknowledged, not a call to accept ongoing mistreatment.
cards.apply_it: In your next disagreement, stick only to the current issue and avoid mentioning any old mistake.

quiz.question: How does Chapman describe forgiveness?
options: A decision not to hold a confessed wrong against someone anymore
Forgetting the wrong ever happened
Pretending you weren't hurt
Waiting until the other person suffers enough
quiz.explanation: Forgiveness is a choice to stop using the past as a weapon.

cards.title: How you say something matters as much as what you say
cards.body:
Chapman notes that the same words can express love or contempt depending on tone. 'I'll help you' said warmly is very different from the same words said with a sigh. For someone whose language is words of affirmation, harsh tone can hurt deeply.

He also suggests that a calm, soft reply can cool an angry exchange. When your partner raises their voice, answering gently and trying to understand their feelings often settles things faster than matching their volume.
cards.apply_it: In your next heated moment, deliberately lower your voice and slow down, and notice the effect.

quiz.question: What does Chapman suggest when your partner speaks angrily?
options: Answer gently and try to understand their feelings
Match their volume so they take you seriously
Leave the room without speaking
Point out that they're being unreasonable
quiz.explanation: A soft response often calms an angry exchange.

cards.title: Listen to understand feelings, not just to fix problems
cards.body:
For people whose language is quality time, Chapman stresses real conversation. He offers practical listening habits: look at the person while they talk, don't do something else at the same time, listen for feelings and not just facts, notice body language, and don't interrupt.

He also warns against rushing to give advice. Often the other person mainly wants to feel understood. If you're not sure, you can ask whether they want suggestions or simply someone to listen.
cards.apply_it: Next time your partner tells you about their day, put your phone away and ask, 'How did that make you feel?'

quiz.question: Which listening habit does Chapman recommend?
options: Plan your answer while they're talking
Do another task to save time
Listen for their feelings, not only the facts
Offer advice as soon as you understand the problem
quiz.explanation: Listening for feelings helps the other person feel understood.

cards.title: Learn to share your own feelings, not only listen
cards.body:
Quality conversation, Chapman notes, runs both ways. Some people find it hard to talk about their own emotions, often because they grew up in homes where feelings weren't discussed.

He suggests a simple exercise: a few times a day, notice a feeling you had, what triggered it, and write it down. Over time, this makes it easier to tell your partner what's going on inside you. Sharing feelings lets the other person know you, not just your schedule.
cards.apply_it: Three times today, note one emotion you felt and what caused it. Share one of them with someone close this evening.

quiz.question: What exercise does Chapman suggest for people who struggle to share feelings?
options: Avoiding emotional topics completely
Noting your emotions and what triggered them during the day
Asking your partner to guess your feelings
Only sharing feelings in writing
quiz.explanation: Tracking emotions builds the habit of talking about them.

cards.title: Do things together that build shared memories
cards.body:
Another form of quality time Chapman describes is shared activities: doing something together that at least one of you enjoys and both are willing to take part in, with full attention on each other.

The activity itself matters less than the togetherness and the memories it creates. A walk, cooking a meal, gardening or visiting a market can become a story you both look back on. Chapman suggests these shared experiences become a store of good memories that a couple can draw on in harder times.
cards.apply_it: Suggest one simple activity to do together this week, and ask your partner to pick the next one.

quiz.question: According to Chapman, what makes a shared activity count as quality time?
options: It must be expensive
It must be something only you enjoy
It must happen on a special occasion
Doing it together with real attention on each other
quiz.explanation: Attention and togetherness matter more than the activity.

cards.title: A gift is a visible sign that you were thought of
cards.body:
Chapman describes gifts as visual symbols of love: something you can hold that says 'they were thinking of me'. He stresses that they don't have to cost much. A flower picked on the way home, a handmade card or a favourite snack can carry as much meaning as something expensive.

For people whose language is gifts, forgetting important occasions or giving carelessly can feel like being overlooked. The thought behind the gift is what they treasure.
cards.apply_it: This week, pick up or make a small, inexpensive gift that shows you know your loved one's tastes.

quiz.question: According to Chapman, what makes a gift meaningful?
options: Its price
The thought it shows
Its size
Whether others see it
quiz.explanation: A gift's value lies in showing you were thought of.

cards.title: Your presence in hard moments is a powerful gift
cards.body:
Chapman describes the 'gift of self': simply being physically there when someone needs you. For many people, especially those whose language is gifts, having a partner present at a hospital visit, a funeral or a big event means more than any object.

He notes how much it can hurt when someone chooses work or other commitments over being there at a crucial time. Showing up, without being asked, can be remembered for years.
cards.apply_it: Is there an upcoming hard or important moment for someone you love? Make a plan to be there in person.

quiz.question: What does Chapman call the 'gift of self'?
options: Buying yourself a treat
Giving away your possessions
Being physically present when someone needs you
Taking time alone to recharge
quiz.explanation: Being there in key moments is itself a gift.

cards.title: If gifts are their language, treat giving as an investment
cards.body:
Chapman observes that people who are careful with money may find it hard to spend on gifts. He suggests a reframe: if your partner's primary language is gifts, buying them thoughtful presents is an investment in the relationship, not money wasted.

This doesn't mean overspending. A small budget used regularly and thoughtfully often matters more than a rare expensive item. He also suggests keeping a list of things your partner has appreciated receiving, to guide future choices.
cards.apply_it: Start a private list of gifts your loved one has enjoyed or mentioned wanting. Set a small monthly amount for thoughtful gifts.

quiz.question: How does Chapman suggest a careful saver think about buying gifts for a gift-loving partner?
options: As an investment in the relationship
As a waste to be minimised
As something only for birthdays
As a way to win arguments
quiz.explanation: Reframing gifts as an investment helps savers speak this language.

cards.title: Help freely given is love; help extracted by guilt is not
cards.body:
For people whose language is acts of service, practical help such as cooking, repairs or taking care of a task speaks loudly. But Chapman is clear that service must be given freely. Help pulled out of someone through guilt, fear or pressure isn't love, and someone who is treated as a doormat is not being loved either.

He argues that allowing yourself to be used can even be unloving, because it lets the other person carry on in a harmful pattern. Real acts of service come from choice and respect on both sides.
cards.apply_it: Notice one task you do for someone out of guilt rather than choice. Could you talk about it openly?

quiz.question: What does Chapman say about service given out of guilt or fear?
options: It's the highest form of love
It's fine if the house stays clean
It's only a problem in marriage
It isn't truly love, which must be freely given
quiz.explanation: Love must be a free choice, not something extracted.

cards.title: Don't let old role expectations block the help your partner needs
cards.body:
Chapman notes that our ideas about who should do which chores often come from the homes we grew up in. One partner may assume certain tasks are 'not my job' because of what their parents did.

If your partner's language is acts of service, those assumptions can keep you from loving them in the way they feel most. Chapman encourages couples to look at those inherited patterns honestly and be willing to change them, so that help flows to where it's actually needed.
cards.apply_it: List three household tasks you assume are your partner's job. Ask yourself where that idea came from, and offer to take one on this week.

quiz.question: Where does Chapman say our ideas about household roles often come from?
options: Our job descriptions
The homes we grew up in
Our friends' advice
Television only
quiz.explanation: Inherited expectations can block acts of service.

cards.title: Learn which kinds of touch your partner actually enjoys
cards.body:
For people whose language is physical touch, Chapman says small, everyday contact matters: a hand on the shoulder, holding hands, a hug when you come home. These are not only about sex; they are about feeling close and connected.

He stresses that people differ. A touch that feels loving to you might feel irritating or uncomfortable to them. The way to learn is to pay attention and ask, and to respect what your partner tells you. Touch is welcome only when it is wanted.
cards.apply_it: Ask your partner gently: 'What kind of affection do you enjoy most?' and listen to the answer.

quiz.question: According to Chapman, how should you learn what touch your partner enjoys?
options: Assume they like what you like
Avoid touch completely to be safe
Pay attention and ask, then respect their answer
Only touch in private
quiz.explanation: People differ, so ask and respect their preferences.

cards.title: In a crisis, a hug can say what words can't
cards.body:
Chapman notes that in moments of grief, shock or fear, many people instinctively reach for each other. A held hand or an embrace can comfort more than any carefully chosen words.

For someone whose primary language is touch, being held in a hard moment can be the clearest sign that they are loved. He also points out the reverse: physical harm or cold refusal of contact can deeply wound someone whose language is touch. Physical violence in a relationship is never a form of love.
cards.apply_it: When someone close is going through something painful, consider offering a quiet hug or held hand, if they welcome it.

quiz.question: Why can touch be especially powerful in a crisis, according to Chapman?
options: It distracts people from their feelings
It's quicker than talking
It shows you're in charge
It can comfort more than words, especially for those whose language is touch
quiz.explanation: In hard moments, welcomed touch speaks deeply.

cards.title: Don't confuse physical desire with a love language
cards.body:
When working out their own primary language, Chapman notes, some people assume it must be physical touch because they have a strong desire for sex. He suggests looking more closely.

If affectionate touch outside of sex, like hugs or holding hands, doesn't mean much to you, your primary language may be something else. A useful test is what makes you feel loved day to day, not just what you desire. Getting this right helps your partner love you in the way that really fills your tank.
cards.apply_it: Ask yourself: apart from intimacy, what makes me feel most loved during an ordinary day?

quiz.question: What test does Chapman suggest for whether touch is really your love language?
options: Whether non-sexual affection like hugs makes you feel loved
Whether you enjoy sex
Whether your partner likes touch
Whether you grew up in an affectionate family
quiz.explanation: Everyday affectionate touch is the better clue than desire alone.

cards.title: Regularly ask: how full is your love tank?
cards.body:
Chapman describes a simple check-in some couples use. One asks the other: on a scale of zero to ten, how full is your love tank? If the answer is low, the follow-up is: what could I do to help fill it?

The game makes it easier to talk about needs without blame. Instead of waiting for frustration to build into an argument, partners get regular, specific information about what would help this week.
cards.apply_it: Try the check-in this week: ask your partner to rate their love tank from 0 to 10 and what one thing would raise it.

quiz.question: What follow-up question goes with the love tank check-in?
options: What could I do to help fill it?
Why is it so low?
Whose fault is that?
How full is mine?
quiz.explanation: The follow-up turns the score into a practical request.

cards.title: Try loving first, even when it isn't returned yet
cards.body:
Chapman tells of couples where love had gone cold. He suggests an experiment: for a sustained period, deliberately speak the other person's love language consistently, even without immediate response, and gently ask what would help.

He reports that this often softens a distant partner over time, because a filled tank makes people more willing to give. It is meant for relationships that are cold or stuck, not for ones that are abusive or unsafe. In those cases, safety comes first, and outside help is needed.
cards.apply_it: If a relationship feels distant, choose one small way to speak their love language every day for a month, and observe what changes.

quiz.question: Who is Chapman's 'love first' experiment meant for?
options: Any relationship, including abusive ones
Only newly married couples
Relationships that have gone cold or distant, not unsafe ones
People who want to make their partner jealous
quiz.explanation: It's for cold relationships; abuse requires safety and outside help.

cards.title: Speaking a new love language feels awkward at first, then gets easier
cards.body:
Chapman compares learning a partner's love language to learning a foreign language. If kind words or physical affection didn't come naturally in your family, expressing them may feel clumsy or forced in the beginning.

His encouragement is to start small and keep practising. Write down a few phrases of appreciation, give a short hug each morning, or set reminders. Like any language, it becomes more natural with use, and the awkwardness is a sign you're stretching, not that you're doing it wrong.
cards.apply_it: Pick the love language that feels least natural to you. Practise one tiny act of it each day for a week.

quiz.question: How does Chapman compare learning a partner's love language?
options: To flipping a switch
To learning a foreign language: awkward at first, easier with practice
To something you are either born with or not
To a test you pass once
quiz.explanation: Like a foreign language, it improves through steady practice.

cards.title: Many people have a strong second love language too
cards.body:
Chapman notes that while most people have one primary love language, many also have a secondary one that matters a lot to them. Some people are almost 'bilingual', valuing two languages nearly equally.

This means that once you've found someone's main language, it's still worth paying attention to the next one. Speaking both, with the primary given the most attention, gives your love more ways to reach them.
cards.apply_it: Ask your partner which two of the five languages matter most to them, and in what order.

quiz.question: What does Chapman say about secondary love languages?
options: Nobody has one
They don't matter
They replace the primary language over time
Many people have one, and some value two nearly equally
quiz.explanation: Many people respond strongly to a second language as well.
